sentences.text: You've left.
This meeting is being recorded.
What was the company that we sold?
Absolute corporate events.
Absolute corporate.
Yeah.
Did you leave?
What happened?
No, no, I'm.
I'm still there.
We rebranded.
Yeah, we rebranded the company into VSpace.
The two.
The acquirer was Venues and Events International.
When we were two years in, we decided to rebrand them, which is now called VSpace.
That's you, you rebranded them.
I bet you talked to me.
I did.
Well, VSpace, it's got Ace at the end from my company and VE at the beginning from the acquiring company.
VE space.
So both names are still in the brand and I figured if I was going to stay around a bit longer, I wanted to make it a bit more sustainable, more interesting.
So, yeah, we did a really nice rebrand, which is now two years ago, but I'm right in there.
Four years now.
That's how long ago that.
Yeah, very, very long time.
Wow.
Okay, well, that's great.
It's good to see that you're still flexing on the whole rebrand thing.
That's.
That's definitely your classic move.
There's.
Yeah, you're right.
Actually there's potentially something coming up though that's a bit more.
A bit more challenging or exciting, which is why I wanted to pick your brains a bit.
Yeah.
Yeah.
I'd love to hear about what's going on, what you're thinking about.
It's obviously a big story, but I'll try and make it as.
As short and high level as I can.
So.
So after the company acquired ace, we went along pretty well.
We had a very successful year and had a very profitable year, mostly coming from my part of the company.
But then I think the investors and the CEO called Anita Low, you may remember Anita, and Bruce was the main investor.
They figured, I think that they'd done such a good job with their acquisition of my company because they did very well out of it, but as did I.
So that's.
We're both happy.

They went on a rapid acquisition trail and since mine bought five more companies, even though my title is chief Strategy Officer and they want me to set the strategy for the business, I don't really do that because they pay no attention to the strategy.
I try and set them.
They just do whatever they like.
So they just randomly bought stuff that didn't really fit so that they now have five other brands as well as the VSpace brand that have not been rebranded yet.
In each has an entrepreneur that's still within the business on earnouts.
It's a bit of a muddle because they've got brands that overlap at best and compete at worst.
There's no, there's no vision, there's no strategy.
Their brands are left ring fenced to do their own thing.

And that might have been okay when there were a couple of them, but now we've got five entrepreneurs in the business now itching for vision and itching to do something, but they're currently thinking of doing is they'll get their own, then they'll go and vspace will make nothing on any of the investments they've made.
Because you make the money after the ear now, as you know, not during the year now.

And there's a bit of a mutiny happening behind the scenes in that a lot of the other entrepreneurs are kind of looking to me to do something about it and what I could do about it is take over and become CEO of the group if the investors in need to let me do that.
But I don't want to do that.
That's not my next step in my plan at all.
But I'm very, very happy to help them do something to change the company around.
And essentially what they need to do is to move Anita out of the role of CEO because she's part of the problem.
She just isn't capable to see a future.
She's 64 now.
She's only ever run the same kind of company, a venue sourcing company, and now she's got these six creative brands.
She doesn't know how to give them what they need and doesn't know how to set a vision for the future.
I do and, and as do the smarter ones of the other entrepreneurs.
So we had some early conversations about a potential mbo and we had a chat with our cfo, our finance director as well, about this.
And just as a side note, this is the seventh finance director this company's had since I joined them.
Wow.
So, which is quite telling in itself that it's not performing well, it's not hit our budget in three years.
Uh, it's scraping through making a couple of hundred thousand ebitdar on a 15 million turnover.
So it's, it's shocking the, the lack of profit it's making.
It's just messy, inefficient.

It's, there's just so much wrong, but it's quite easy to put right if you just change the leadership structure and set a vision because there is some great talents and great people in there and there's a potential for it to be very, very profitable.
So that's Kind of where we are.
So the structure would have to be a new CEO.
I think Anita would need to stick around.
She owns 30% of the business and the other two investors own 70%.
So I think an MBO would need to buy the 70% of the investors to get them out.
Let Anita stay in, move her behind the scenes to be a chairman and then I'd actually cut the business in half because there are two very different types of branches brands within the company.
There's some corporate meetings brands and some creative events brands.
And I'd create two divisions and brand them separately because they're very different clients, very different markets and very different cultures.
And there's, there's a clear and obvious CEO in the business for each of those two divisions.
Kim in the venues, in the kind of corporate side and then a guy called Lee on the creative side who's got a potential but not ready yet.

So if we were to do it, then I would step up of CEO of the creative side for the first year to two and move Lee into that role so that we would be credible from day one and able to affect it straight away.
So that's kind of the plan in a nutshell.
As far as there's a couple of things that make it difficult in that there's one big earn out that's only in its first year and it's the most successful of all the brands she's got.
It's a brand called we love this.
And they've got three years of earnouts due.
The first one at the end of this year.
I don't know how you would tackle an earn out with due an awful lot of money in a mbo because one of the first things I'd want to do is mix all the brands up.
Leaving them separate and ring fenced prevents us doing the best with the business plan.
Another brand called Chilled, we only own half of it.
The other half is still owned by the the previous owner.
And they did this ridiculous deal where at the end of three years each of them have an option to buy the half but they're not forced to buy the other half.
So they could just be in stalemate.
So I don't know how to fix that dilemma either.
Because we only own half of that company.
I'd like to have all of it because it fits really well with the plan.

So on the creative side, I'd create one brand with all the companies, all the talent together and that would be the, that'd be the, the sweetest, most profitable part of the Business going under the brand.
We love this.
Is that what you're thinking?
I don't know what I'd call it yet.
It would, it would have.
I think what I'd do is create an umbrella brand for the current brands as they are for the.
To begin with, and then migrate them into the umbrella brand over time.
So I wouldn't want to just throw the brands away.
That they're all very strong.
On the creative side, you've got chilled.
The two main ones are chilled.
And we love this.
They're really the two lead brands.
On that creative side.
They're both pretty good brands, but they don't need their brand units.
Brands are cosmetic in beta and B2B really, as you know.
But the most important thing is getting them to work together because that way I can make the economies of scale because the duplication of effort and talent across the brands too, it's just a mess.
They would work much better as one.
So there's these complications that I don't know how to address those.
And then the other thing is value.
Because if the company returned a profit of about 200,000 last year and this year it's likely to raise between 2 and 500,000, it's not worth very much.
But the investors have got much, much higher price tags in mind.
They think the company's worth between 5 and 10 million.
There was nothing like that.
You know, nobody's going to put even maybe a million in because you could sell on the potential.
I'm fairly confident that that 200000 profit EBITDA could easily be 2 million within three years, which.
Then why are they.
Without going into it too much.
But why are.
Why are they only making such a small margin?
Are they just.
They've got no eye whatsoever that they overspend everywhere.
Anita's background is she's a salesperson, so she only really understands top line and cash.
She doesn't really understand profit or margin.
And so the costs are just not controlled at all.
Out of 130 people, there's 17 in the finance department.
That in itself is absolutely insane.
You know, there's.
It's twice the size it should be.
There's no investment on systems to make things more efficient because they, they're afraid of spending money but yet they spend thousands.

So if I can't get 20 grand to buy a system that will save 10 people because they look at 20 grand as a cost and they can't spend it, they won't give me 30 grand to invest in AI to cut out all process.
That means I could get rid of a team of 30 people because they see 30,000 as a big ticket item that they don't understand.
Cost versus investment.
So they spend a lot of money on people and they're hugely inefficient, but they actually are delivering events with very good margins.
They're just spending it all on.
On people and ridiculous costs.
We've got eight offices all over the uk.
We don't need them because all the people would rather work at home anyway.
It's, you know, I could go on and on and on, but literally in the first year, I could create profit out of what they've got.
There's no need to make new business.
It's all there in the business.
It's just massively inefficient.
So what, do you have any access to capital at all, Chris, or investors yourself?
I don't, no.
So, I mean, the difficulty is always going to be the valuation of the business today, isn't it, to be able to leverage any kind of investment against the 200k.
You're going to be struggling.
The only thing that is obviously quite attractive is that there is 15 million right at the top of the top of the business.
But that doesn't create evaluation.
No.
The good thing, though, Andrew, is I. I think the investors have kind of had enough of her now.
I think they really want out.
And I don't know the details of the finances, but I did ask Anita, when she was a bit tipsy, whether Bruce had had his money back or if he hadn't, what was he owed and how much had he had he back?
And she wouldn't tell me, but she said, he's had his money back.
And I said, well, give me an idea.
Has he had twice his money back or five or ten times his money back?
And she said, it's more like 10 times had 10 times his investment backs.
I don't think he put much in back in the day.
Maybe a couple of hundred, if that.
And the dividends he's had over the years while they were making money before they invested in all these companies, I think he's had his money back.
I also think he's got no confidence in her ability to drive the company forward anyway.
So I don't think it would cost much at all to buy the 70% of the company that we want.
And it's almost better to do it while it's not making much money and while he sees there's no future in it, because giving him a fairly small check might make them go away.
If we can get 70% of the company and I'm wondering, in my mind, I'm thinking a million might buy them both out.
A million for 70% of the company.
So there's, there's two shareholders that own the 70.
Yeah, yeah.
Bruce has got most of it.
So Bruce has got 50, John's got 20 and then each and her husband have got 30.
There's around figures.
It's not exactly that basically it's there or thereabouts.
So we'd be raised, looking to raise a million on an EBITDA of somewhere between 2 and 500,000.
If it's nearer 500,000 then that I guess is an easier sell.
But if it's only 200 again, then you've got a company that's made 200 grand for two years running.
So you're thinking find a million in cash to pay them out on day one.
I think that will be the best way to do it.
I think we'd want the MBO parties to put something in as well.
So maybe the.
I think, I'm thinking there's either four or five of us would be the MBO team.
I'd expect us to at least put in 250,000.
So you're then looking at VC or other capital of 750.
But that still doesn't solve my problem about the earnouts and the other half of the company that we don't own because I'd need, I don't know how to address that.

I either give the people that have got earnouts a bigger share in the new company that recognizes the value of what they're giving up, but I don't want my hands tied by their earn out deal because it means I can't do anything with the business for three years.
One doesn't mean not anything overdramatic.
It really restricts how much is owned.
Oh, do you know what the amount is for the three year old to.
This that is with it?

I think there's probably, and I'm guessing from what I've heard 1.2 to 1.5 million total over three years, which I think the company could make that to pay it back to them over the three years might not be at the same rate that they're expecting.
But the other problem is right now the company's got massive cash flow problems and that they literally are juggling with cash every day because there's not enough to go around.
So they're delaying payments and if we don't do something, I'm not sure the company will last a year because they're spending so much money and not making enough.
They've just taken a loan from the bank of half a million for working capital and the investor has guaranteed that loan.
So they've got cash flow problems.
Yeah.
Have you thought about prepack?
Would they liquidate?
Would they do something along those lines?
Don't know.
I hadn't thought about that.
So you could do a recapitalization through a prepack.
So basically the leadership, the directors, current directors, would have to put it through a liquidation process.
But what you would do is you set that up with you guys as the buyers of the prepackaged business already with the liquidators.
And so you buy it for a song basically out of the back end.
They put it into liquidation.
You, you pick up the assets for close to nothing.
And that would save the whole MBO process.
Anita would obviously have to be on board, but she would benefit for taking 30 out the back, I guess with you as a partner and she sits as chairman.
But you would be able to shake out the current investors.
They would have to take a minimum amount of whatever the assets are worth to the liquidators.
And the liquidators don't really care.
They just need to look at what are the current debts on the balance sheet and can you raise enough capital to pay out those, those people.
So your 250k for instance, that could be enough to do the whole thing.
Choice wouldn't be my first choice because reputational impact would be difficult to get over.
And also Anita's done that before in her past and still suffers with that reputation because she left a lot of hotels without money and then set up again the day after with a slightly different name.
The idea with the pre pack is actually you pick everything up.
You know, you pick everything up.
Any debts.
I mean, if you've got loads of creditors, then obviously that could be an issue if they're your clients for whatever reason or you need to continue to, to deal with them as vendors afterwards.
Obviously you don't really want to do that.
But, but that would be the, that would be the, the smartest move possibly if you are in cash flow crisis.
The problem is the owners of we love this would resist that and wouldn't support that because then they lose because their business ring fenced is very profitable.
All the profit is coming from them and has been spent by the rest of the business.
And if they let that happen, then their earnout is dead too.
So they've got the most leverage out of everybody.
Then they have they have under the newest in.
In that they're not even a year old yet.
I mean, this already looks a bit scary, I will say, because straight off the bat, you can't even afford out of your own profits to pay for.
We love this.
That's.
I mean, that's the first thing that is clear.
Why did she do that deal?
I mean, how did she raise the capital to, to do that deal in the first place?
Every deal has been financed by a company cash flow.
Yeah, but there is no, there's no cash flow left.
There isn't now.
That's why.
So what?
She staged all the deals to be paid in three steps, just like mine.
If you remember, I was paid out of my own cash flow.
So I hit all my profit targets and then she wrote a check from my bank account to pay for me.
And because that worked, she's used that same model for all the other acquisitions.
But they've not all been as successful as mine or they've not all kept their promises.
I kept mine.
So the model starts to fall apart.
And this is what I can see in what the future looks like now is the business won't have enough money to pay for the remaining trenches unless it is there.
You know, I could just go and see it now and say, let me fix the business and do it, but there's no gain in that for me apart from to balance a shitload of work.
And I'm not going to do that.

Is there a, is there a conversation to be had there, Chris, that you could fix the business and that you could become an investor in the business either through sweat equity or just some kind of agreement that the fix is, are your, are your share that you would gain over a period of time or is the, the only thing is I'm looking at this, is it.
Because it's not very profitable.
The, the leverage for, for more debt is difficult to justify.
I mean, the lenders are going to look at this and go, well, well, why, why would it make sense for us now to risk our money?
Because you, you actually need too much almost.

You know, if you're saying if you've got 250k, that's good, but let's just say that it's worth 3x because that's what you would probably get from sub 1 million EBIT to business, then you can only really leverage 600k against 100 of the business.
So if she is still maintaining 30, then you're not even there on the debt side of things.
That's only 400k?
Pretty much.
We could get the profit up this year because our financial year runs at the end of March, so we're only halfway through the financial year.
If we get the profit nearer to a million this year by me making.
Some mistakes, that changes everything.
Yeah, that changes everything.
What does the profit need to be for it to change it sufficiently to make it look better?
If last year's profit was 200k, if this current year was X, what would X need to be, do you think?
Well, for the math to stack up, you need to be around 500k EBIT, don't you?
Because that would get you to 1.5 million on a, on a 3x which would give you enough cash for any to continue to earn 30% and they need to leverage the rest for debt.
Okay, I think I can make that happen.
So at the moment I'm deliberately not doing anything because I'm thinking keep the company worth as little as possible because then it's easier to buy.
But if there's, it's one of the reasons I wanted to chat with you.
So if there's a point it's got to be at to make the numbers work, then that mean I can make that happen.
I could make this.
But I also wonder, Chris, whether you've got leverage yourself there to get some kind of toehold on the shareholding.
I mean, it's definitely a conversation to be had, I would say.
I mean if you could negotiate.
A.

Percentage from all of them, maybe just like 10% of the business, but to take a bit from everybody and say, look, this business needs turning around, there is nobody else that can do it except me, but I want to take 10% to do it.
That's an option.
I guess the only that just makes means that I'm stuck with the same investors who are part of the problem and stuck with Anita in role of CEO who is also part of the problem.
So part of that would have to be the investors would need to back down because they currently interfere too much and not in a positive way.
They're kind of on the same level as Anita and they are the problem.

Is there any way of, I mean, obviously it's a scary conversation, but is there any way of saying to Anita, look, Anita, I'm happy to step into see a role and you would be able to step into a chairman role which would be better for you after, you know, years of running the business.
I, I keep playing that in my head.

Well, there's two, there's two scenarios I keep auditioning in my Head one is that one and the other is going to Bruce, the main investor, and having a conversation with him because I think he would, he asked me about a year and a half ago if I was willing to step up if he had her removed and I just said no.
But things weren't as bad as they are now or things didn't look as bad as they, they look now.
And I just thought, I don't need it.
I'm just going to coast for another couple of years and then go do something else.
So I think I'm wondering whether a conversation with him is a better one because I think he thinks that door is closed now.
But if I suggested to him that it was.
Yeah, I think so.
And I wonder with him being.
If he removed Anita rather than I.
Suggested it, with him being majority shareholder as well, would he be able to drag along the, the 20% shareholder?
Yeah, the other investor will do whatever Bruce says.
He controls that other stuff.
So potentially as well, you could issue more shares to you in, in some way if you were to agree to do it, because they would have to cast invoke to be able to do that.
So I think it looks like the best option for now.
You've definitely got a six month window where you need to get the house in order.
Yeah.
If you're going to raise the finance against the business because currently it's just too small.
Yeah, okay.
No, I get that.
I see that.
So most important thing is get that profit up to 500,000 this year and then think about who to have the conversation with.
Yeah.
As early as possible.
Really?
It sounds like if you could push Anita out quickly and take over the reins as CEO, then that would give you a lot more control of the business, wouldn't it?
Regardless of any shareholder.
And you've got Bruce's, you've got his ear at the moment.
Yeah, yeah.
But I think that you need to, I think you need to get a shareholding in it as soon as possible so that it's worth your while.
Otherwise just fixing it for somebody else.
Exactly.
And once it's fixed, it's too late to ask.
Yeah, exactly.
And you've made it more valuable and more expensive for you to get in at that point as well.
Of course.
Okay, that's very, very helpful.
Yeah, I hope so.
I hope so.
It is, it is.
If, if that happens, then if, if none of those routes prove effective, I don't get the right response from either of them.
Is it at the right level that you think that it's possible to Raise the capital to do an mbo.
If I've got investors in Anita, that won't play along but they would have to do if we did an mbo.
Yeah.
I think there's a few different ways you could go.
Certainly the fact that you can raise 250k yourselves pretty good.
I think you could also go and find investors to invest in you.
You've got a great, great track record.
You've exited twice before.
It makes sense.
You know, this is a ready rolled roll up that hasn't been, you know, the value hasn't been extracted yet, particularly this last acquisition that's gone in.

But basically they act more like investors than a bank lending money.
So it's much more risky capital and they're used to the risk but they want to see that you can turn this around and you've got a track record to explain it.
So the only thing is right now it's just, it's too small from a profit point of view.
But the fact that you've got 50 million turnover, if you can show that actually all of that's just being wasted and it, you know, the events themselves are profitable, the gross margin is.
Is there and the net would be there if they were.
We're not free everything on overhead then.
Then I think you've got a good conversation to have.
Yeah.

With private debt, which would be more interesting for you because it would be, you know, investors that were ready to go with you and you could sell all of this to private equity in three to five years.
Yeah.
To make the savings, turn it into a profitable roll up and then sell it onto private equity.
Yeah.
So that all makes sense.
Yeah, definitely.
I go that route.
Is that's something you're able to help me with to find those kind of investors?
Yeah, we know private, private debt.
There's quite a few different ones that we could be talking to.
Yeah, for sure.
And they love this space.
They, they like marketing live comms.
So.
Yeah, definitely.
Okay, I will give it lots of thought.
Yeah.
I'll send you the recording to this from Fireflies because you can dump into chat GPT and grill it and it's all there for you.
Brilliant.
Appreciate it.
All right, good to see you again anyway.
Yeah, you too.
Thanks so much for that.
I really appreciate it.
Yeah, no worries.
Let me know what you're thinking.
Get back to me in a few weeks and let me know what you're thinking of.
Absolutely.
All right.
No worries.
Speak to.

summary.overview:
- Chris Parnham's company, Absolute Corporate Events, rebranded as VSpace post-acquisition by Venues and Events International, has faced operational inefficiencies due to a fragmented brand strategy and lack of unified vision.
- Leadership issues stem from ineffective CEO Anita Low, whose limited capabilities led to operational inefficiencies and a lack of strategic direction amidst a complex company structure with multiple entrepreneurs.
- Chris proposes a management buyout (MBO) to acquire 70% of investor ownership, aiming to restructure into two divisions with separate CEOs, initially leading the creative side himself.
- Financial challenges include persistent cash flow issues, with only £200k EBITDA generated from £15 million turnover, showing the necessity for immediate restructuring.
- Key brands like 'We Love This' and 'Chilled' hinder restructure efforts due to earn-out agreements and partial ownership, limiting flexibility despite their profitability.
- The company is facing a cash flow crisis, necessitating a £500k working capital loan and frequent payment juggling due to expense overrun and staffing inefficiencies.
- Discussions included potential recapitalization strategies through pre-pack administration, which poses reputational risks and challenges with profitable earn-out owners.
- Chris estimates that acquiring the 70% investor stake would cost roughly £1 million and could be partially financed by contributions from the MBO team.
- Chris aims to improve EBITDA from £200k to £500k within six months to bolster attractiveness for financing and facilitate a transition to CEO and restructuring plan.
- Andy suggests
summary.short_summary: The discussion highlighted critical leadership restructuring needs, as Chris Parnham described a dysfunctional state with six separate brands lacking a unified strategy, leading to inefficiencies. CEO Anita Low, who owns 30%, is perceived as part of the problem, while investors owning 70% have made random acquisitions that alienate entrepreneurs. Chris is under pressure to take action, with plans to replace Anita and split the company into two divisions led by Kim and initially by Chris, transitioning to Lee. Financially, the group is underperforming with a mere £200,000 EBITDA on a £15 million turnover, raising concerns about the feasibility of a management buyout. Existing earnout agreements complicate restructuring, and raising capital is crucial yet hindered by low profitability and investor dynamics. Immediate steps include improving profitability and negotiating leadership changes within six months.
